passage:
Note from Amandeep, class teacher:
At home time, Chandrika was near the gate when a man she did not know said, "Come, I have sweets. Your mother sent me." She looked at the sweets, then at me, frowning, and pulled at her bag strap. Then she said "No," ran to me and told me what he had said. I kept her beside me, told her she had done nothing wrong, and alerted the gate guard, the head teacher and her mother. Next day I taught the class: refuse, go straight to a grown-up you trust, and tell them. Any grown-up wanting a child's secret or favour is a warning sign.

qa.q: What did the man say to Chandrika at the gate?
qa.a: He said, "Come, I have sweets. Your mother sent me."

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling when she looked at the sweets and then at Amandeep?
qa.a: She seemed tempted and confused, since she frowned and pulled at her bag strap before deciding.

qa.q: What rule did Amandeep teach the class the next day?
qa.a: Refuse, go straight to a grown-up you trust, and tell them, because any grown-up wanting a child's secret or favour is a warning sign. 🤍

qa.q: How might Chandrika's mother see what Chandrika did?
qa.a: She would probably feel relieved and proud that Chandrika said no and told the teacher, as she was told straight away.

grounding: A stranger offers sweets and claims the mother sent him; the child feels confused, says no, runs to a trusted adult and tells.
